title: Four Beasts, the Ancient of Days, and the Son of Man
summary: Daniel sees four terrible beasts rise from a storm-tossed sea, the last with ten horns and a boastful little horn. Then thrones are set, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, the court sits in judgment, and the beast is destroyed. One like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom, which an interpreter explains is given to the saints of the Most High after a time of persecution.
story:
This is the hinge of the book. It is the last chapter written in Aramaic, the language that runs from 2:4 to 7:28, and so it completes the unit that began in chapter 2, whose four-part statue it retells as four beasts. But it is also the first of Daniel's own visions, turning from stories about him (chapters 1 to 6) to revelations given to him (chapters 7 to 12). It steps back in time to the first year of Belshazzar, before the banquet and fall of Babylon in chapter 5, so the reader who has just watched Daniel survive the lions under Darius now sees what Daniel had seen years earlier.

Where chapter 2 showed the kingdoms as a statue admired by a king, chapter 7 shows them as God sees them: predatory beasts. Where chapter 2 ended with a stone cut without hands, this chapter ends with a person, one like a son of man, who receives the kingdom from God and shares it with God's holy people. The stories of chapters 3 and 6 showed faithful Jews delivered from kings who demanded worship; this chapter widens the lens to show that the whole sequence of empires is under judgment and that God's people may suffer before they are vindicated. The visions of chapters 8 to 12 all build on this one, narrowing its focus to a single persecuting king.
historical:
Belshazzar's first year was probably about 553 BC. Babylonian texts explain why he is called king. His father Nabonidus (556 to 539 BC), the last king of Babylon, left the city for the oasis of Tema in Arabia and stayed about ten years. The Verse Account of Nabonidus says that before leaving he entrusted the kingship to his eldest son, and the Nabonidus Chronicle notes year after year that the king was in Tema while the crown prince remained in Babylonia with the army. The empire still looked secure, but Cyrus of Persia had begun the rise that would bring Babylon down in 539 BC.

The four beasts are explained only as four kings or kingdoms (verses 17 and 23). The first, a lion with eagle's wings that is made to stand like a man and given a human mind, is taken by interpreters of every school as Babylon, recalling Nebuchadnezzar's humbling in chapter 4; the prophets had pictured Babylon's king both as a lion (Jeremiah 4:7; 50:17) and as a great eagle (Ezekiel 17:3, 12). The traditional Jewish and Christian reading takes the bear as Media-Persia (raised on one side because Persia came to dominate the Medes), the four-headed leopard as Greece (Alexander's swift conquests from 334 to 323 BC and the kingdoms into which his generals divided them), and the fourth beast as Rome. That reading is already present in 4 Ezra 12:11-12 (late first century AD), which says the eagle of its own vision is the fourth kingdom shown to Daniel, in Josephus (Antiquities 10.276), and in the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 2b). Most critical scholars read the bear as Media, the leopard as Persia, and the fourth beast as the Greek empire of Alexander and his successors, with the ten horns as rulers of the Seleucid line in Syria and the little horn as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 to 164 BC). Futurist interpreters add that the little horn, or a figure it foreshadows, is a final antichrist still to come. The pattern of four world empires followed by a fifth was not unique to Daniel: a Roman writer, Aemilius Sura, quoted in Velleius Paterculus (Roman History 1.6.6), lists Assyria, Media, Persia, and Macedonia before Rome.

The details of the little horn fit Antiochus IV closely, which is the main reason for the critical reading. He came to the throne in 175 BC past others with a better claim, including his nephew Demetrius, then a hostage in Rome. In 167 BC he outlawed the Sabbath, the festivals, circumcision, and the temple sacrifices, and in the month of Kislev that year an altar to a foreign god was set up on the altar of burnt offering (1 Maccabees 1:41-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-11), a direct attempt to change the appointed times and laws (verse 25). Judas Maccabeus rededicated the temple in Kislev 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52), about three years later, and Antiochus died on campaign in Persia the same year. Those who hold the traditional date answer that the chapter's scope is larger than one king and that its fourth kingdom is better matched by Rome's reach and endurance; the question of the book's date is set out in the book introduction and in the second hard question below.

The book was widely read in the period between the testaments. Eight manuscripts of Daniel were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, more than for most books of the Hebrew Bible, and the oldest, 4QDan c, has been dated to the late second century BC. An Aramaic text from Qumran (4Q246) speaks of one who will be called son of God and whose kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, language drawn from this chapter and 2:44.
cultural:
The sea churned by the four winds draws on an image shared across the ancient Near East: the sea as the realm of chaos and hostile power. In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, Marduk defeats Tiamat, the salt sea, before creating the world; in the Canaanite myths known from Ugarit (a coastal city in Syria destroyed around 1200 BC), the storm god Baal wins kingship by defeating Yam, the sea. The Old Testament uses the same imagery of God's victory over the sea and its monsters (Psalm 74:13-14; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9-10; Job 26:12). Hermann Gunkel's Schöpfung und Chaos (1895) made this background central to modern study, and J. A. Emerton (Journal of Theological Studies, 1958) argued that Daniel 7 reworks the Ugaritic pattern, in which the aged high god El, called ‘father of years’, presides over the divine council while the younger Baal, ‘rider of the clouds’, receives kingship. Others think the biblical imagery of Psalm 104 and Ezekiel 1 is enough to explain the scene.

Beasts that combine features of different animals were familiar from Babylonian and Assyrian art. Great winged bulls and lions with human heads guarded Assyrian palace gates, and in Babylon itself the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way built by Nebuchadnezzar were faced with glazed-brick lions, bulls, and the dragon of Marduk. To a reader in Babylon, the vision took the empire's own symbols of power and turned them into monsters. Horns were the standard image of strength and royal power (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 75:10; Zechariah 1:18-21), so a beast with ten horns is a power with many kings, and a horn with eyes and a mouth is a king who sees and speaks with arrogance.

The heavenly courtroom uses royal and legal imagery. Israel knew the picture of God enthroned among his council (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 82:1; Job 1:6). Thrones are set, the judge takes his seat, and attendants number thousands upon thousands; “The court was convened, and the books were opened” (verse 10), the records by which the court decides, like the book of remembrance in Malachi 3:16 and the books of the dead in Revelation 20:12. The plural thrones puzzled later readers: the Babylonian Talmud (Hagigah 14a; Sanhedrin 38b) reports that Rabbi Akiva explained them as one for God and one for David, that is, the Messiah, and was rebuked for it. The Ancient of Days, an aged figure with clothing white as snow and hair like wool, conveys dignity, wisdom, and eternity, since gray hair was honored as the crown of a long and righteous life (Proverbs 16:31; 20:29). His fiery throne with wheels recalls Ezekiel's vision of God's chariot-throne (Ezekiel 1 and 10), and the river of fire recalls the fire that surrounds God at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:11-12).

The phrase son of man (bar enash) in Aramaic ordinarily means simply a human being, like the Hebrew ben adam by which God addresses Ezekiel more than ninety times. What is remarkable is that this human figure comes with the clouds of heaven, which elsewhere in the Old Testament are the vehicle of God himself (Deuteronomy 33:26; Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1), and that all peoples ‘serve’ him (pelach), a verb Daniel otherwise uses for the worship of God or the gods (3:12, 14, 17, 18, 28; 6:16, 20). The phrase ‘a time, and times, and half a time’ (verse 25), which returns in 12:7 and Revelation 12:14, is usually taken as three and a half years, half of seven, a limited and broken period. Revelation expresses the same span as forty-two months and 1,260 days (Revelation 11:2-3; 12:6; 13:5).
literary:
The chapter is an apocalyptic vision followed by an interpretation, the pattern for the rest of the book. An apocalypse, from the Greek word for unveiling, is a revelation given through a heavenly mediator that discloses both the heavenly world and the course and end of history. Daniel sees, is troubled, asks one of the heavenly attendants, and receives an explanation. The vision itself alternates between earth and heaven: beasts rising from the sea (verses 2 to 8), the court in heaven (verses 9 and 10), the beast destroyed (verses 11 and 12), and the son of man enthroned (verses 13 and 14). The heavenly scenes are written as poetry, in balanced lines, while the beasts are described in prose. A refrain of seeing (‘I kept watching’, chazeh havet) marks each new scene (verses 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13, and 21).

The interpretation comes in two rounds, a brief one (verses 17 and 18) and a longer one focused on the fourth beast and the little horn (verses 19 to 27). The second round adds details not in the vision, such as the bronze claws and the horn's war against the saints, so that the explanation deepens the vision rather than merely decoding it. The chapter ends not with Daniel's understanding but with his distress: he turns pale and keeps the matter to himself (verse 28).

The chapter's great contrast is between beastly rule, which devours and tramples, and human rule, which receives its kingdom from God. The first beast is lifted to stand like a man and given a human mind, as Nebuchadnezzar was restored in chapter 4, but the others only grow more monstrous, until a truly human figure appears from heaven's side. The pattern reverses Genesis 1, where humanity is made to rule over the beasts; here beasts have seized rule, and God restores it to one like a son of man. Adrien Lenglet (Biblica, 1972) showed that the Aramaic chapters form a mirrored arrangement: chapters 2 and 7 on four kingdoms, 3 and 6 on faithful Jews delivered from death, and 4 and 5 on God's judgment of proud kings. Chapter 7 therefore closes the circle the statue opened, and the Hebrew chapters that follow expand its last kingdom in detail.

In the Hebrew Bible, Daniel stands not among the Prophets but among the Writings, the third section of the canon, while the Greek and Christian Bibles place it with the prophets after Ezekiel.

outline.t: Four beasts from the sea and the little horn
The Ancient of Days and the court in heaven
One like the Son of Man receives the kingdom
The fourth beast, the little horn, and the saints

doctrines.note: The kingdom that replaces the empires belongs to God, is given to the son of man, and is shared with “the saints of the Most High” (verses 18, 22, 27). It is everlasting and universal, the opposite of the beasts' borrowed and temporary dominion, and it is received rather than seized. This chapter is the main Old Testament source of the Gospels' language of the kingdom of God given to the Son of Man.

History is not left to the beasts. A heavenly court sits, the books are opened, the arrogant power is condemned, and the other beasts lose their dominion (verses 10 to 12, 26). God's judgment is presented not as a threat to the faithful but as the necessary condition for justice to the oppressed: the Ancient of Days “pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High” (verse 22).

The kingdom is given to one like a son of man, a human figure who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion. Later Jewish readers, from the Similitudes of Enoch and 4 Ezra to the Talmud and Rashi, took him as the Messiah, and Jesus claimed the title for himself.

The son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion, glory, and kingship (verses 13 and 14). The New Testament sees this enthronement fulfilled when the risen Jesus ascends and is seated at God's right hand, with all authority given to him (Matthew 28:18; Mark 14:62; Acts 7:56).

The saints are handed over to the little horn for a limited time before the court acts (verses 21 and 25). The vision does not promise escape from persecution but a limit to it, a judge over it, and a kingdom beyond it. Daniel himself is not comforted by the vision but troubled (verse 28), which gives believers permission to be shaken by what they know.

words.note: Enash, man, mankind, the Aramaic counterpart of Hebrew enosh. It occurs about twenty-five times, all in the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra. Joined with bar (son) in verse 13, bar enash is an ordinary Aramaic way of saying a human being, and in later Aramaic it could also mean ‘someone’ or be used of oneself. Its force here comes from the contrast with the beasts: God's kingdom is given to a figure who is truly human, not beastly, yet who comes from heaven's side. The same word describes the lion made to stand like a man and given a man's mind (verse 4).

Bar, son, the Aramaic word that appears in Psalm 2:12 in Hebrew form and in names like Barnabas and Bartholomew. In the phrase bar enash it does not mean literal descent but belonging to a class: a son of man is a member of humankind, as sons of the prophets are members of a prophetic guild. The phrase has no article in verse 13, so it is ‘one like a son of man’, a comparison and not yet a title. In the Gospels, where Jesus says ‘the Son of Man’ with the article, it has become a title that points back to this figure.

Attiq, ancient, advanced in age, found only three times in the Bible, all in this chapter in the title Ancient of Days (verses 9, 13, 22). The standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) give ‘advanced, aged’. The title portrays God as eternal and venerable, the judge who was there before every empire and will be there after them. Later Christian tradition, especially in the East, often identified the Ancient of Days with the Son, as the note on the chapter's history explains.

Qaddish, holy, holy one, the Aramaic counterpart of Hebrew qadosh. It occurs thirteen times, all in Daniel. In 4:13, 17, and 23 it names an angelic watcher, and some scholars, notably John Collins, argue that the ‘holy ones of the Most High’ here are angels too. Most interpreters read them as God's faithful people on earth, since they are persecuted and defeated by the little horn (verse 21) and are called ‘the people of the holy ones’ in verse 27. Some take the phrase to include both, the heavenly host and the earthly people who share its cause.

Sholtan, dominion, rule, the word behind the modern title sultan. It occurs fourteen times, all in the Aramaic of Daniel. The beasts' dominion is taken away (verses 12 and 26), while the son of man receives “an everlasting dominion that will not pass away” (verse 14), echoing the praise of Nebuchadnezzar and Darius for God's everlasting dominion (4:3, 34; 6:26). The chapter is a contest over who truly holds dominion, and the answer is God and those to whom he gives it.

Malku, kingdom, kingship, reign. It occurs about fifty-seven times, all in the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra, and is the key word of the Aramaic chapters: kingdoms rise, are divided, pass to others, and are taken away. In this chapter it names both the four earthly kingdoms and the kingdom given to the son of man and the saints, which will never be destroyed (verses 14, 18, 27; compare 2:44). The Greek equivalent, basileia, is the word Jesus uses for the kingdom of God.

Pelach, to serve, pay reverence. It occurs ten times, nine of them in Daniel and once in Ezra 7:24 (for temple servants). In Daniel it is the verb for worship: the three men refuse to ‘serve’ Nebuchadnezzar's gods (3:12, 14, 18) and Darius says Daniel ‘serves’ his God continually (6:16, 20). When all peoples serve the son of man (verse 14) and all rulers serve the Most High's kingdom (verse 27), the language implies more than political submission, which is one reason many interpreters see the figure as sharing divine honor.

Qeren, horn, the Aramaic counterpart of Hebrew qeren. It occurs fourteen times, in Daniel 3 for the musical horn and in this chapter for the horns of the fourth beast. In the Old Testament a horn is a symbol of strength and royal power (Psalm 75:10; 1 Samuel 2:10), so the horns are kings (verse 24). The little horn with eyes and a boastful mouth becomes the central figure of chapters 7 and 8 and supplies imagery for the beast of Revelation 13, which has ten horns and a mouth uttering blasphemies.

christ:
Jesus' favorite way of referring to himself was the Son of Man, a phrase found about eighty times in the Gospels and almost only on his own lips, and this chapter is its main source. At first the phrase sounds modest, simply ‘a human being’, and Jesus used it of his humble work and coming suffering: “even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), a saying that deliberately reverses verse 14, where all peoples serve him. He also used it of his authority, to forgive sins on earth (Mark 2:10) and to judge, since the Father “has given Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man” (John 5:27).

At his trial, when the high priest asked whether he was the Christ, Jesus answered, “I am,” and added, “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62), joining Psalm 110:1 to verse 13. The high priest heard it as blasphemy, because Jesus was claiming the place beside God that Daniel gives to the one who comes with the clouds. Jesus also spoke of the Son of Man “coming in the clouds with great power and glory” (Mark 13:26), and after his resurrection he declared, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (Matthew 28:18), language close to verse 14. Stephen at his death saw “the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56), the one figure in heaven who stands to receive a suffering saint.

The chapter's pattern of suffering followed by vindication also shapes the Gospels. The saints are handed over and then given the kingdom; the Son of Man, Jesus said, must suffer many things and be rejected and then rise (Mark 8:31). Revelation describes the risen Christ as “One like the Son of Man” (Revelation 1:13) with hair white like wool, a feature Daniel gives to the Ancient of Days (Revelation 1:14), so that the one who receives the kingdom shares the appearance of the one who gives it. Revelation 11:15 announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and Revelation 13 draws its beast from the sea, with ten horns and a boasting mouth, from this chapter. The New Testament reads verses 13 and 14 as a real prophecy of the Messiah's enthronement, while also seeing the saints share his kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:2; Revelation 20:4), which honors the chapter's own link between the son of man and the people of the holy ones.
interpretation:
The chapter shaped Jewish hope before the New Testament. The Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37 to 71, probably first century BC or AD) describe a preexistent ‘Son of Man’ who sits on a throne of glory and judges, and 4 Ezra 13 (late first century AD) sees a man rising from the sea and flying with the clouds, identified as God's Son and Messiah. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) reconciles Daniel's Messiah on the clouds with Zechariah's king on a donkey: if Israel is worthy he will come with the clouds, if not, lowly. Rashi read the son of man as the King Messiah and, in the next verse, as Israel, whom he represents; many other Jewish commentators take the figure as the people of Israel. Daniel is never read as a synagogue prophetic reading, since it belongs to the Writings.

Hippolytus of Rome wrote the oldest Christian commentary to survive complete, on Daniel, around AD 204, reading the fourth beast as Rome and the little horn as the antichrist. The Neoplatonist Porphyry, in the twelfth book of his Against the Christians (late third century), argued that Daniel was written under Antiochus Epiphanes and described the past, not the future. His argument survives because Jerome quoted and answered it in his Commentary on Daniel (about 407), which defended the Roman reading. Byzantine art sometimes painted Christ himself as the Ancient of Days, and the Moscow council of 1666 to 1667 declared that the Ancient of Days was the Son, forbidding icons of the Father as an old man.

Luther's preface to Daniel (1530), written as the Ottoman army besieged Vienna in 1529, read the little horn as the Turk, and Calvin's lectures on Daniel (1561) followed the Roman reading while warning against speculation. The Fifth Monarchy Men of 1649 to 1660 took Daniel's fifth kingdom as a call to prepare England for Christ's reign, and Isaac Newton's Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel (published 1733) treated the chapter as a key to history. Modern scholarship has focused on the son of man: Gunkel and Emerton traced the imagery to ancient myth; Maurice Casey (Son of Man, 1979) argued the figure symbolizes Israel; John Collins (Hermeneia, 1993) identified him with the archangel Michael; and Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012) argued the vision presents a second divine figure beside the Ancient of Days.

In worship, the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 9 and 10 and 13 and 14 on Christ the King Sunday in Year B and verses 1 to 3 and 15 to 18 on All Saints' Day in Year C. William Blake's The Ancient of Days (1794), the frontispiece of Europe a Prophecy, borrowed Daniel's title for a figure of his own mythology, and Robert Grant's hymn O Worship the King (1833) sings of the Ancient of Days, pavilioned in splendor.
text:
Daniel 7 is written in Aramaic, the international language of the Babylonian and Persian empires, and its verse numbers are the same in Hebrew and English Bibles. Readers will still meet several differences.

The capital letters of verse 13 are an interpretation. The Aramaic has no article and no capitals: ‘one like a son of man’. The BSB, NASB, and NKJV print “One like the Son of Man”, signaling the Christian reading; the ESV has ‘one like a son of man’, and the NRSV and some Jewish translations ‘one like a human being’. The same holds for ‘saints’ or ‘holy ones’ of the Most High, where translations choose between the traditional word and a more literal one.

The Greek versions differ in ways that shaped the New Testament. Two ancient Greek translations of Daniel exist: the Old Greek, preserved in Papyrus 967, Codex Chisianus (manuscript 88), and the Syriac of the Hexapla, and a later version attributed to Theodotion, which replaced the Old Greek in the church's Bibles. In verse 13 Theodotion has the figure coming ‘with the clouds’ and reaching ‘up to the Ancient of Days’, while the Old Greek has ‘on the clouds’ and says he came ‘as the Ancient of Days’, with attendants waiting on him; scholars debate whether that reading arose from a scribal confusion or a deliberate interpretation. Mark 14:62 has ‘with the clouds’, and Matthew 24:30 and 26:64 have ‘on the clouds’. In verse 17 both Greek versions read ‘four kingdoms’ rather than ‘four kings’, and several English translations follow them, since verse 23 explains the fourth beast as a kingdom. Papyrus 967 also arranges the book in a different order, placing chapters 7 and 8, dated under Belshazzar, before chapters 5 and 6.

teach.big: However monstrous the powers of the world become, they rise and fall under the judgment of the eternal God, who gives the everlasting kingdom to the Son of Man and to his suffering saints.

outline.t: Seen from heaven, the great empires are not noble statues but devouring beasts, and the worst is the one that speaks arrogantly against God.
Above the chaos sits the Ancient of Days: thrones are set, the books are opened, and the beasts' power is judged and removed.
God gives lasting dominion not to a beast but to one like a son of man who comes with the clouds and whom all peoples serve.
The vision is given for understanding, and its first word to the troubled believer is that the saints will receive the kingdom forever.
Persecution is real and may seem to prevail, but it is limited in time, answered by God's court, and followed by the kingdom given to his people.
Revelation does not remove distress; Daniel is shaken and keeps the matter in his heart, and faith can live with that.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misuse of this chapter is to treat it as a code for current events, identifying the ten horns with a modern alliance or the little horn with a living politician. Interpreters have done this in every century, from the Turks in Luther's day to the European Common Market in the 1970s, and each identification has faded. The chapter's own interest is theological: who rules history, what arrogant power looks like, and what God will do about it. Teachers can present the major identifications of the beasts fairly without staking the lesson on one of them.

A second misreading keeps only verses 13 and 14 and skips the beasts and the suffering, as if the vision promised quick triumph. The interpretation dwells on the little horn's war against the saints (verses 21 and 25); the kingdom comes after persecution, not instead of it. A third flattens the son of man into a mere symbol or, on the other side, preaches Jesus from verse 13 without letting the reader see why the figure was already striking in its own setting: human, yet coming with the clouds and receiving service reserved for God. Finally, avoid using the chapter to baptize a nation or party as the kingdom of the saints. In Daniel every human empire, including the one that sheltered Daniel, is a beast; the kingdom that lasts is received from God.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to believers who live under hostile governments or who suffer for their faith, and to anyone frightened by the direction of the world. Teach it as Daniel received it: God does not hide the beasts, and he gives a limit to their power and a court above them. It also speaks to those who assume faith should bring calm. Daniel receives the clearest vision of God's victory in the book and is left pale and troubled (verse 28), so no one in the room should be told that fear or distress means they lack faith. Be careful with listeners drawn to anxious end-times speculation; point them to what the chapter plainly teaches rather than feeding the anxiety.

hard.q: Who is the one like a son of man, and was he ever meant to be the Messiah?
hard.a:
The strongest objection to the Christian reading comes from the chapter itself. The interpreter never mentions the son of man; instead, the kingdom is given to “the saints of the Most High” (verses 18 and 22) and to “the people, the saints of the Most High” (verse 27). Since the beasts stand for kingdoms, many scholars conclude that the human figure stands for a people. Maurice Casey (Son of Man, 1979) argued that the figure is a symbol of faithful Israel and that when Jesus used bar enash he meant it in its ordinary Aramaic sense, the explicit references to Daniel being added by the early church. Many Jewish interpreters have likewise read the figure as the people of Israel. John Collins (Hermeneia, 1993) takes another route, identifying the son of man with an angel, most likely Michael, Israel's heavenly prince (10:21; 12:1), and the holy ones as the angelic host, since in Daniel heavenly beings often appear ‘like a man’ (8:15; 10:16, 18).

The traditional Jewish and Christian reading answers that a king in the ancient world could stand for his people, just as the beasts are called both kings (verse 17) and kingdoms (verse 23), so the son of man can be an individual whose kingdom his people share. It points to what sets the figure apart: he comes with the clouds, as only God does, and receives service that Daniel elsewhere reserves for God. That individual reading appears early, in the Similitudes of Enoch and 4 Ezra, in Rabbi Akiva's explanation of the thrones, in the Talmud's Messiah who comes with the clouds (Sanhedrin 98a), and in Rashi. N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) reads the figure as Israel's representative, vindicated after suffering, and argues that Jesus took that role on himself. Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012), writing as a Jewish scholar, argues that the vision presents a second divine figure enthroned beside the Ancient of Days and that this expectation was at home in Judaism before Jesus. These readings are not entirely exclusive, and the New Testament holds several together: Jesus is the Son of Man who receives the kingdom, and his saints reign with him.

hard.q: Was this chapter written in the sixth century BC as a prediction, or in the second century BC about events already under way?
hard.a:
The critical case is strong and old. The Neoplatonist Porphyry argued in the third century that Daniel was composed under Antiochus Epiphanes and that its prophecies are accurate up to his reign and not beyond, and most modern scholars, including James Montgomery (International Critical Commentary, 1927) and John Collins (Hermeneia, 1993), agree. They note that the little horn's actions match Antiochus in detail, that the visions grow sharper as they approach 167 BC and then turn general, that the Hebrew Bible places Daniel among the Writings rather than the Prophets, and that the book's Hebrew, Aramaic, and loanwords fit a later date. On this view the chapter is not deception but a recognized form, like other Jewish apocalypses written in the name of an ancient seer, meant to assure persecuted Jews that God's plan was on schedule. Some evangelical scholars, such as John Goldingay (Word Biblical Commentary, 1989), accept the second-century date and argue that it does not diminish the book's authority.

Defenders of a sixth-century setting, among them E. J. Young (The Prophecy of Daniel, 1949) and Joyce Baldwin (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, 1978), answer that the book presents itself as Daniel's first-person visions, that Jesus spoke of the abomination ‘spoken of by the prophet Daniel’, that the Aramaic resembles other official Aramaic of the Persian period, and that the chapter's fourth kingdom fits Rome better than Greece, since Media and Persia were a single empire (8:20) and Rome's reach and endurance exceed Greece's. They also note that manuscripts found at Qumran, the oldest from the late second century BC, show the book already copied and revered soon after the date critics propose. Ernest Lucas (Apollos, 2002) sets out both cases carefully. The question involves how prophecy works and what kind of writing an apocalypse is, and faithful readers answer it differently. On either view the chapter's claim stands: God rules over the empires, judges the arrogant, and gives the kingdom to the one like a son of man.

observe: Describe each of the four beasts. What does each one do, and what is done to it?
What details does the interpretation in verses 19 to 27 add that were not in the vision itself?
What words describe the kingdom given in verses 14, 18, and 27? How are they different from the words used of the beasts?
interpret: Chapter 2 pictured the kingdoms as a statue; chapter 7 pictures them as beasts. What does the change of image teach about how God sees human power?
Why is it significant that the one who receives the kingdom is ‘like a son of man’ yet comes with the clouds of heaven?
How do verses 21 and 22 hold together the saints' defeat and their vindication, and what does the court scene add?
apply: Where are you tempted to be either awed or terrified by the powers of your own day, and how does the throne scene of verses 9 and 10 change that?
The saints suffer for a limited time before the court sits. How does knowing that suffering has a limit, and a judge, help you or someone you know endure it?
Jesus called himself the Son of Man, the one who came to serve before he was served. What would it look like to follow that pattern this week?
